appraisal_events.evidence: "Ce fut un long défilé, mais un défilé devant le baron seul"; "Personne n'eût plus pensé à se faire présenter à Mme Verdurin"; he credits her only as the page who armed Joan of Arc; inviting only M. Verdurin to the Duras soirée was "le plus sanglant outrage pour l'épouse."
appraisal_events.explanation: Throughout his own party Charlus positions himself as the sole object of the guests' gratitude and attention while structurally excluding and patronizing his hostess; the narrator explicitly calls the culminating slight to her the most bloody insult.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Il est immonde"... "Il paraît qu'il a fait de la prison"... "il est dans les griffes de ce Jupien... qui le fait marcher au bâton et lui fait cracher tout l'argent qu'il veut."
appraisal_events.explanation: Enraged by her exclusion, Mme Verdurin retaliates by inventing lurid accusations against Charlus to enlist Brichot in a plot to separate him from Morel; the narrator flags this as fabrication ("un certain don d'improvisation quand la malveillance l'inspirait"), so the vilification is reported rather than endorsed as fact.

status_effects.explanation: She is systematically ignored, unrecognized by departing guests, and structurally excluded from credit at her own salon.
Guests form a long line paying homage exclusively to him and treat him as sole author of the evening's success.
He is verbally cast as a criminal and blackmail victim in a conversation staged to undermine him, though the narrator frames these claims as malicious invention rather than fact.
She successfully overcomes Brichot's hesitations and enlists his complicity, gaining leverage to execute her plan against Charlus.

ambiguities: Mme Verdurin's accusations against Charlus (prison record, criminal associations, blackmail by Jupien) are explicitly framed by the narrator as invented slander rather than endorsed fact, so E2 registers her rhetorical assault and its social leverage rather than a narratorial verdict on Charlus's actual conduct.
